And I was exposed to directors like Takashi Miike, who did Audition and Ichi the Killer, and films coming out of South Korea like Sympathy for Mr. Vengeance. And I just thought, oh my God, what the hell is going on in these Asian countries that they are making the movies this violent? And what I saw was that American movies try to play it safe, American horror movies. They don't want to offend people. And so the kind of directors like Miike understand that what makes a great horror movie is that it lives in that danger zone, that dangerous territory. And it harkens back to kind of Italian cinema in the 70s, films like Cannibal Holocaust or Pasolini's Salo, where they're making movies that are so violent, but they're not trying to please everybody. They're not for everybody. They're for a very specific audience. They're like, this is a sick movie. If you don't like it, stay the hell away from it. And I just felt like nobody was doing anything like that in America. So that's what I wanted to do. And I also like the fact that the Asian films aren't really pure. They're not really pure. They're not exactly pure horror movies. It's not like The Garage or The Ring. There's a wave of these ultra-violent films that are much more horrific than scary. It's about real people doing real things, and they're just horrifying and disturbing. And that's the type of horror that I like.
